nodes.claim: For peak firing rate, 79.3% of delay-act and 72.3% of delay-sup cells showed significant correlation with delay length; for mean firing rate, 34.5% and 37.3% respectively (p=0.01, permutation test).
nodes.verbatim_quote: a substantial fraction of units demonstrating a significant correlation between firing rate and delay length (mean firing rate, 20/58 [34.5%], peak firing rate, 46/58 [79.3%] for delay-act; mean firing rate 31/83 [37.3%], peak firing rate, 60/83 [72.3%] for delay-sup; p=0.01, permutation test

strengths: Both peak and mean firing rate correlations are examined, showing different sensitivities.
Permutation testing (p=0.01) confirms that the observed percentages exceed chance.
The distinction between peak and mean firing rate as measures is thoughtful and acknowledged by the authors.
weaknesses: The very high percentages for peak firing rate correlations (79.3% and 72.3%) are striking but may be inflated: peak firing rate mechanically increases with longer recording periods in longer delays due to sampling variability, creating a systematic positive correlation artifact.
The authors note 'mean firing rates at different delay lengths will result in deformative normalization' but do not fully address whether peak firing rate has analogous biases.

The sample sizes (58 delay-act, 83 delay-sup) represent subsets of the total 639 neurons — presumably those recorded across all five delay conditions — but the selection criteria for this subset are not entirely transparent.
The p=0.01 permutation test for percentages is reported for both categories combined; individual category significance is unclear.
alternative_interpretations: Peak firing rate correlations with delay length could be a statistical artifact of longer sampling windows yielding higher maximum rates, rather than reflecting true rate coding of delay length.
required_assumptions: Peak firing rate is not systematically biased by the duration of the observation window.
Neurons were stably recorded across all five delay conditions (sequential sessions).
evaluation.notes: The potential confound of peak firing rate scaling with observation window duration is a significant concern that is not addressed.

nodes.label: SVM decoding of delay length from population spikes was significantly above shuf…
nodes.claim: SVM decoding of delay length from population spikes was significantly above shuffled controls across five animals (F2=882.1, p<0.001, two-way ANOVA).
nodes.verbatim_quote: Red **: observed vs neuron shuffled, p<0.001; magenta **, observed vs neuron and condition shuffled, p<0.001; group effect, F2=882.1, p<0.001, two-way ANOVA.

strengths: SVM decoding with leave-one-trial-out cross-validation is a reasonable approach.
Comparison against two shuffled controls (neuron-shuffled and neuron+condition-shuffled) strengthens the interpretation.
The highly significant F-statistic (F2=882.1) provides strong evidence of above-chance decoding.
Data from five animals are included.
weaknesses: The number of neurons varies substantially across animals (17-43), and it is unclear how this affects decoding performance.
The absolute decoding accuracy is not reported in the main text — only the ANOVA comparing observed vs. shuffled is given.
With only ~10 trials per condition, the training set is small, which could affect reliability.

The finding that delay length can be decoded 'even prior to delay initiation' complicates the interpretation — this could reflect different behavioral states or running speeds rather than delay-length encoding per se.
alternative_interpretations: Pre-delay decoding of delay length could reflect behavioral correlates (e.g., running speed, anticipatory behavior) that co-vary with delay condition rather than neural encoding of delay information.
Since conditions are run in blocks (sequential delay extension), the decoder might be capturing slow drift in neural activity rather than delay-specific coding.
required_assumptions: Neural activity patterns are not confounded by systematic behavioral differences across delay conditions.
The sequential block design does not introduce temporal confounds into the decoding analysis.
evaluation.notes: The block design (sequential delay extension) is a concern for decoding analyses, as time-varying factors could masquerade as delay-specific coding.

nodes.label: About 10% (4/33) of delay-act cells initially fired after reaching the goal in 0…
nodes.claim: About 10% (4/33) of delay-act cells initially fired after reaching the goal in 0 s delay, then shifted to firing during the delay period once delay was introduced, and did not return to goal-related activity when delay was eliminated.
nodes.verbatim_quote: about 10% (4/33) of delay-act cells initially fired after the animal reached the goal in the 0 s delay condition, then shifted their firing to the delay period once a delay was introduced

strengths: The observation of experience-dependent shifts in firing is consistent with Gill et al. (2011) findings of learning-dependent hippocampal activity.
The irreversibility of the shift (not returning to goal-related activity) is an interesting observation.
weaknesses: Only 4/33 neurons showed this pattern — too few to draw strong conclusions.
No statistical test is provided for this specific observation.
It is unclear whether these 4 neurons were tracked reliably across sessions or whether this could reflect different neurons being recorded.
The interpretation of 'shifted firing' versus 'different neuron sampled' is difficult to distinguish with extracellular recording across sessions.
alternative_interpretations: Electrode drift between sessions could result in recording different neurons, creating the appearance of a firing shift.
The small number (4/33) is within the range of chance occurrences and may not represent a meaningful phenomenon.
required_assumptions: The same neurons were reliably tracked across sessions with different delay conditions.
The 4 neurons are representative of a biologically meaningful subpopulation.
evaluation.notes: The authors appropriately describe this as 'about 10%' rather than making strong claims, but the evidence is still quite thin.

nodes.label: The log ratio of firing rates (large/small reward) was significantly different b…
nodes.claim: The log ratio of firing rates (large/small reward) was significantly different between delay-act and delay-sup cells under both reward loss (Z=-2.6, p=0.007) and reward gain (Z=2.1, p=0.03) conditions.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the log ratio of the firing rates (large reward/small reward) under both reward loss and gain conditions was significantly different between delay-act and delay-sup cells (Z = −2.6, p=0.007 for reward loss; Z = 2.1, p=0.03 for reward gain, Mann-Whitney's U-test)

strengths: Both reward loss and reward gain conditions are tested, providing bidirectional evidence.
The statistical tests are appropriate (Mann-Whitney U) for comparing the two cell populations.
The effect is consistent across two independent manipulations (loss and gain), strengthening the interpretation.
Source data is made available.
weaknesses: The sample sizes for the reward manipulation conditions are not explicitly stated in this part of the text.
The p-values (0.007 and 0.03) are modest, particularly for the reward gain condition.
The order of reward manipulations (loss first, then gain) could introduce order effects, though the authors attempt to address this with the opposite-flow control.
alternative_interpretations: The differential responses could reflect motivational state changes rather than reward-specific coding.
The classification into delay-act and delay-sup groups was done independently of reward manipulation — the observed differences could partly reflect regression to the mean.
required_assumptions: The animals' motivational state was comparable across reward loss and gain conditions.
The delay-act/delay-sup classification is stable across reward manipulations.
evaluation.notes: The bidirectional design (loss and gain) is a strength of the experimental approach.

nodes.label: One-sample t-tests confirmed negative skew in delay-act cells (T=-2.5, p=0.01) a…
nodes.claim: One-sample t-tests confirmed negative skew in delay-act cells (T=-2.5, p=0.01) and positive skew in delay-sup cells (T=2.7, p=0.01).
nodes.verbatim_quote: the ratio was negatively skewed in the delay-act cells (T = −2.5, p=0.01, one-sample t-test) but positively skewed in delay-sup cells (T = 2.7, p=0.01, one-sample t-test

strengths: The one-sample t-tests against 0 are appropriate for testing whether the distributions are shifted.
Both populations show significant effects in opposite directions, consistent with dissociable coding.
The effect sizes appear reasonable given the reported T-statistics.
weaknesses: The use of 'skew' in the text is imprecise — the one-sample t-test tests whether the mean differs from zero, not whether the distribution is skewed in the statistical sense.
The p-values are both exactly 0.01, which is marginally significant and would not survive stringent multiple comparison correction.
The underlying distributions of firing rate ratios are not described — if non-normal, the t-test may not be appropriate.
Sample sizes for these specific analyses are not clearly stated.
alternative_interpretations: The mean shift could be driven by a small number of outlier neurons rather than reflecting a population-level property.
required_assumptions: The distribution of firing rate ratios is approximately normal, or the sample is large enough for the t-test to be robust.
The ratio metric (large reward / small reward) is the appropriate measure for this comparison.
evaluation.notes: The terminology 'negatively skewed' and 'positively skewed' appears to refer to the sign of the mean rather than statistical skewness, which could confuse readers.

nodes.label: Under forced conditions with unrewarded delay, CA1 neurons indicating choice pre…
nodes.claim: Under forced conditions with unrewarded delay, CA1 neurons indicating choice preference were silent, and firing re-emerged when preference recovered to the rewarded side.
nodes.verbatim_quote: When faced with an unrewarded delayed option, CA1 neurons indicating choice preference were silent.

strengths: The forced-choice paradigm is a creative design to observe activity for less-preferred options.
The result is consistent with the interpretation that delay-act neurons encode subjective value.
weaknesses: No quantification or statistical analysis is provided — only the qualitative statement that neurons 'were silent'.
Only example neurons are shown (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), with no population-level analysis.
The number of neurons and animals contributing to this observation is not reported.
The forced-choice condition introduces multiple confounds (barrier, stress, frustration) that could affect firing independent of value coding.
The claim that 'firing re-emerged when preference recovered' is described in the figure supplement but not statistically tested.
alternative_interpretations: Silencing of neurons under forced conditions could reflect the animal's awareness that a barrier is present (a spatial/contextual change) rather than value coding.
Stress or frustration from forced choice could globally suppress firing in certain populations.
required_assumptions: The forced-choice paradigm does not alter the spatial or contextual variables that CA1 neurons encode.
The observed silencing is specific to value/preference rather than behavioral state changes.
evaluation.notes: This is presented as evidence for subjective value coding but lacks the quantitative rigor needed to support that interpretation.

nodes.label: 73.5% (114/155) of delay-act and 64.9% (124/191) of delay-sup neurons showed sig…
nodes.claim: 73.5% (114/155) of delay-act and 64.9% (124/191) of delay-sup neurons showed significant side-selectivity under three-way ANOVA (side × delay-length × timing).
nodes.verbatim_quote: The percentage of side-selective neurons was high in both CA1 delay-act (114/155: 73.5%) and delay-sup(124/191: 64.9%) neurons

strengths: Three-way ANOVA (side × delay-length × timing) is an appropriate statistical approach for assessing side-selectivity.
Large sample sizes (155 delay-act, 191 delay-sup neurons) provide adequate power.
The use of switched and both-side conditions to assess spatial selectivity is well-designed.
The finding that ~25-35% of neurons encode delay independent of location is an important result.
weaknesses: Given that hippocampal neurons are well-known place cells, finding that ~70% are side-selective is not surprising and the high percentage could partly reflect the spatial code rather than a specific delay-location interaction.
The criteria for determining side-selectivity from the three-way ANOVA are not fully specified — it is unclear which main effects or interactions were used to classify a neuron as side-selective.
Confidence intervals are provided but no effect sizes for the ANOVA results.
alternative_interpretations: The high percentage of side-selective neurons could simply reflect underlying place cell properties rather than an integration of delay and spatial information.
Side-independent neurons (~25-35%) may represent a distinct functional subpopulation or may simply have bilateral place fields.
required_assumptions: The three-way ANOVA appropriately separates spatial from temporal and delay-related contributions.
Recording the same neurons across switched and both-side conditions is reliable.
evaluation.notes: The finding that a substantial minority of neurons encode delay independent of location is perhaps more novel and interesting than the majority that show spatial selectivity.

nodes.label: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant genotype effect (F1=14.4, p<0.001) and genoty…
nodes.claim: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant genotype effect (F1=14.4, p<0.001) and genotype × delay interaction (F4=23.0, p<0.001), with cKO mice showing significantly higher large-reward preference at delays 5-40 s.
nodes.verbatim_quote: F1 = 14.4, p<0.001, genotype (CA1-NR1cKO vs NR1 f/f); F4 = 23.0, p<0.001, interaction between delay length x genotype

strengths: The two-way ANOVA with genotype × delay interaction is appropriate.
The significant interaction (p<0.001) demonstrates that the genotype effect is delay-dependent, as expected for a delay discounting deficit.
Post-hoc comparisons at each delay length provide detailed information about where the effect emerges.
No difference at 0 s delay (p=0.61) demonstrates that basic reward preference is intact.
weaknesses: The F-statistic notation is unusual — 'F1 = 14.4' and 'F4 = 23.0' appear to omit denominator degrees of freedom.

The interaction F-statistic is reported as 'F1,4 = 1.07, p=0.37' which appears to be non-significant, contradicting the claim that there is a significant genotype × delay interaction. The F4 = 23.0 appears to be the delay main effect, not the interaction.
Sample sizes for cKO (n=8) and control (n=9) groups are relatively small for behavioral studies.
The sequential design of delay extension could interact with learning differences between genotypes.
alternative_interpretations: The cKO mice may have impaired learning of delay contingencies rather than altered delay discounting per se.
The behavioral phenotype could be interpreted as reduced behavioral flexibility or perseveration rather than lower delay discounting.
Given the authors' own acknowledgment that NR1 deletion may extend beyond CA1 by the testing age, the behavioral effect may not be CA1-specific.
required_assumptions: The CaMK2-Cre driven NR1 deletion is primarily affecting CA1 at the time of behavioral testing.
Motivational and sensory processing are comparable between genotypes.
evaluation.notes: There is an apparent contradiction in the reported statistics: F4=23.0 (p<0.001) is labeled as 'interaction between delay length x genotype' but F1,4=1.07 (p=0.37) also appears to be an interaction term. This needs clarification — the reported statistics may contain an error.

nodes.label: The ratio of delay-act/delay-sup cells was significantly lower in cKO compared t…
nodes.claim: The ratio of delay-act/delay-sup cells was significantly lower in cKO compared to control mice (p=0.02, Fisher's Exact Test).
nodes.verbatim_quote: the ratio of delay-act/delay-sup was significantly lower in the cKO than in the control mice (Figure 8C, p=0.02, Fisher's Exact Test

strengths: Fisher's Exact Test is appropriate for comparing proportions.
The result is consistent with the behavioral deficit observed in cKO mice.
weaknesses: The sample sizes are quite small (cKO n=3 mice, 123 units; control n=4 mice, 69 units), with significant clustering by animal.
Fisher's Exact Test treats each neuron as independent, but neurons within an animal are not independent — this violates the assumption and could inflate significance.
The control group has fewer total units (69) than the cKO group (123), making direct comparison of proportions potentially problematic.
95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals are mentioned but the actual proportions for each genotype are not clearly stated in the text.
alternative_interpretations: The different proportions could reflect differences in electrode placement or recording quality rather than a genuine biological difference.
With only 3 cKO and 4 control mice, individual animal variation could drive the group difference.
required_assumptions: Neurons from different animals within a genotype can be pooled and treated as independent observations.
Recording quality and electrode placement were comparable between genotypes.
evaluation.notes: The non-independence of neurons within animals is a significant statistical concern for this claim. A mixed-effects model or animal-level analysis would be more appropriate.

nodes.label: Delay-act cells in cKO mice showed non-specific activation during the delay peri…
nodes.claim: Delay-act cells in cKO mice showed non-specific activation during the delay period, and their temporal distribution was sparse and not specific to delay-onset.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Delay-act cells in the cKO mice showed non-specific activation during the delay period...the temporal distribution of all delay-act cells in the cKO was sparse and not specific to delay-onset.

strengths: Population vector analysis provides a visual comparison between cKO and control mice.
The qualitative difference in temporal distribution is evident from the figures.
Example neurons from cKO mice are shown with non-specific activation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
weaknesses: The characterization of activity as 'non-specific' and 'sparse' is largely qualitative with no formal statistical test comparing temporal distributions between genotypes.
Only 3 cKO animals contribute to this analysis, making it susceptible to individual animal effects.
No statistical test is provided to compare the population vector segmentation between genotypes.
The term 'not specific to delay-onset' is vague and not quantified.
alternative_interpretations: The 'non-specific' activation could reflect that the few delay-act neurons identified in cKO mice are simply place cells with fields overlapping the delay zone, rather than delay-coding neurons.
With fewer delay-act cells in cKO (as per c1.6.2.1), the temporal distribution analysis has less power and the 'sparseness' could be a sample size artifact.
required_assumptions: The same classification criteria applied to control mice are appropriate for cKO mice despite potential differences in firing patterns.
The qualitative comparison of population vectors is meaningful without formal quantification.
evaluation.notes: This claim would benefit from quantitative statistical comparison between genotypes rather than relying on visual comparison of figures.

nodes.label: The firing rate ratio of cKO delay-act cells was significantly different from co…
nodes.claim: The firing rate ratio of cKO delay-act cells was significantly different from controls and lacked the negatively skewed distribution (Z=2.0, p=0.04, Mann-Whitney's U-test).
nodes.verbatim_quote: the ratio of CA1 firing of cKO was significantly different than that observed in control mice and lacked the expected negatively skewed distribution (Z = 2.0, p=0.04, Mann-Whitney's U-Test

strengths: The Mann-Whitney U test is appropriate for this comparison given likely non-normal distributions.
The result is consistent with the broader pattern of disrupted value coding in cKO mice.
weaknesses: The p-value (0.04) is marginal and would not survive correction for multiple comparisons across all genotype comparisons made.
Small sample sizes (3 cKO mice, 4 control mice) again raise concerns about generalizability.

The comparison is between the firing rate ratios of delay-act cells specifically, but the delay-act classification may itself be different between genotypes (as noted in c1.6.2.1), potentially confounding the comparison.
The neuron non-independence issue (neurons nested within animals) applies here as well.
alternative_interpretations: The difference in firing rate ratios could reflect differences in how delay-act cells are classified in cKO mice (i.e., different populations are being compared) rather than a genuine disruption of value coding.
required_assumptions: The delay-act classification identifies comparable functional populations in cKO and control mice.
The reward manipulation was conducted comparably in both genotypes.
evaluation.notes: The marginal p-value and small animal sample sizes make this result suggestive but not definitive.

nodes.label: No significant differences in mean firing rate between genotypes: overall (cKO 3…
nodes.claim: No significant differences in mean firing rate between genotypes: overall (cKO 3.07 Hz vs control 3.39 Hz, p=0.44), delay-act (p=0.35), or delay-sup (p=0.14).
nodes.verbatim_quote: mean firing rate, cKO — 3.07 Hz, control — 3.39 Hz, Z = −0.76, p=0.44, Mann-Whitney's U-test

strengths: Testing basic firing properties rules out the possibility that the genotype effects on delay coding are simply due to altered excitability.
Three separate comparisons (overall, delay-act, delay-sup) are provided.
The non-significant results are clearly reported with exact p-values.
weaknesses: Non-significant p-values do not prove equivalence — a Bayesian or equivalence test would be more informative.
The p=0.14 for delay-sup subpopulation firing rates approaches marginal significance and might indicate a trend worth noting.
The same neuron non-independence issue applies.
alternative_interpretations: Absence of evidence for a difference is not evidence of absence — the comparison may be underpowered.
required_assumptions: Mean firing rate is a sufficient summary statistic for 'basic firing property' comparisons.
The Mann-Whitney U test has adequate power to detect meaningful differences given the sample sizes.
evaluation.notes: This is an important control analysis. The limitation is the standard caveat about null results in frequentist statistics.

nodes.label: The ages of cKO animals in the recording sessions were slightly more than 2 mont…
nodes.claim: The ages of cKO animals in the recording sessions were slightly more than 2 months old, beyond the age at which NR1 deletion is restricted to CA1 pyramidal cells.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Physiological characterization, however, may have harbored a more widespread deletion of the NR1 gene as the ages of cKO animals in the recording session were slightly more than 2 months old

strengths: The authors transparently acknowledge this limitation.
The specific timeline of Cre-mediated recombination is referenced (Fukaya et al., 2003).
This caveat is appropriately placed in the methods and discussed further in the discussion.
weaknesses: This caveat significantly weakens the interpretation of all cKO physiology results (c1.6.2.1 through c1.6.4.1) because the NR1 deletion may extend to CA3, dentate gyrus, and deep cortical layers.

The exact ages of the cKO animals used for recording are referenced (Table 5) but not stated in the main text, making it difficult for readers to assess the extent of this concern without consulting supplementary materials.
alternative_interpretations: Any physiological differences observed could be due to NMDAR loss in regions other than CA1, such as CA3 input deficits or cortical dysfunction affecting hippocampal inputs.
required_assumptions: The primary effect of the NR1 deletion on the observed phenotypes is mediated through CA1 pyramidal cells.
evaluation.notes: This is a significant caveat that the authors acknowledge. It means that claims about CA1-specific NMDAR requirements should be interpreted with caution. This caveat applies to c1.6.1.1, c1.6.2.1, c1.6.3.1, and c1.6.4.1.

summary.overall_assessment: The paper's 48 claims show mixed overall support when weighted by centrality (weighted support score 0.60, where the central thesis counts far more than peripheral evidence). The most load-bearing weakly-supported claim is: “A specific subset of CA1 neurons fit the criteria of value coding, responding in the same way to delay length changes and reward size changes.” (7 weakly-supported claim(s) total).
